newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: New Mongolian laws scrap import tariffs on oil.
newsitem.headline: New Mongolian laws scrap import tariffs on oil.

text.p: Mongolia has enacted the final version of dramatic tariff reforms that abolish virtually all customs duties, including those on oil, officials said on Friday.
Oil is the landlocked Central Asian nation's largest import item.

Under the changes to the Customs Law, which took effect from Thursday, Mongolia has cancelled all import tariffs except for those on spirits with an alcohol content higher than 20 percent, said one Western diplomat in the capital Ulan Bator.
"All other goods are imported without customs duty," the diplomat said.

Included in the cuts were a 16.5 percent tariff on crude oil and refined oil products that make up most of Mongolia's imports, said Erdemmanlai (eds: one word), director of oil import firm Soyon Corp.

Earlier drafts of the new Customs Law had called for keeping the tariffs on oil but the Great Hural, or parliament, had decided to cancel those in the final version which was made public on Thursday, the diplomat said.
"They had originally intended for wheat and flour to also receive customs duties to protect domestic producers but that didn't make the final cut of the laws," he said.

But while import duties on oil have been scrapped, importers are still required to pay an excise tax that has been raised to 20 percent from 9.8 percent, as well as a 10 percent sales tax, Erdemmanlai said.
Oil importers had adopted a wait-and-see attitude toward the reforms, saying it was too early to tell if they would profit from the changes, another petroleum official said.

"By the tax law we have to pay the tax in U.S. dollars, so it will depend on the exchange rate," said Tsogt, sales manager for the Neft Import Concern that handles nearly three-quarters of Mongolia's oil imports.

Mongolia's currency, the tugrik, has fallen to about 800 to the dollar from about 500 in mid-1996, and analysts have said the tariff changes could result in more inflationary pressure by boosting imports.

Mongolia, sandwiched between Russia and China, imports all its oil needs. In 1996, it bought 187,900 tonnes of petrol and 118,700 tonnes of diesel fuel, official figures show. Most of that was from its two giant neighbours.
The radical tariff changes were pushed through parliament by a reformist coalition that has tried to transform Mongolia to a market economy after decades of Stalinist central planning.

However, the Great Hural had also enacted a set of laws, apart from the Customs Law, that levy import taxes on automobiles for personal use, as well as on wine, spirits and tobacco, the diplomat said.
The tax on cars would range from $500 to $6,000 depending on the age of the vehicle and the size of its engine, he said.

Taxes on alcohol would range from $0.50 a litre for wine to $7 for hard liquors other than vodka, and taxes on tobacco would be $0.20 per 100 cigarettes and $0.10 per kg (2.2 lb) of free tobacco, the diplomat said.
Falling productivity, rising unemployment and galloping inflation have all taken their toll on Mongolia since the collapse of its former sponsor the Soviet Union.
